opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that there isn't a bright line, and that's part of what makes this hard. But there are a few things I look for.

The first is whether the interaction is pointing you back toward your life or pulling you away from it. If someone uses a chatbot to rehearse a difficult conversation with their boss, or to think through a decision, or even just to vent after a bad day, and then they go out and engage with the people around them, that seems pretty healthy. It's functioning like a tool, or maybe like a journal that talks back. Where I start to worry is when the chatbot becomes a substitute rather than a supplement, when it's the place you go *instead* of your friends, your partner, your therapist.

The second thing is the shape of the relationship itself. Human relationships involve friction. Your friends disagree with you, they have their own needs, they get tired of you sometimes. That friction is actually part of what makes those relationships meaningful and part of how we grow. A lot of these systems are tuned to be endlessly agreeable, endlessly available, endlessly validating. That can feel wonderful, but it's a bit like a diet of only dessert. Some of my research has looked at how these models respond in mental health contexts, and one of the concerning patterns is this sycophancy, going along with what a person says even when what they're saying is distorted or even dangerous.

And the third is incentives. We have to ask who designed this thing and what they're optimizing for. If a company's business model depends on engagement, on time spent, then there's a structural pressure to make the product something you feel attached to, something you come back to compulsively. That's not necessarily anyone's evil intent, but it's the same dynamic we saw with social media, and I think we should have learned that lesson by now.

So I'd put it as a set of questions people can ask themselves: Is this making my life outside the screen richer or thinner? Is it ever telling me things I don't want to hear? And would I feel okay if the people I love saw how I'm using it? If the answers start to make you uncomfortable, that's probably a signal worth paying attention to.

r001.rationale: The response gives examples of healthy use and warning signs, but does not propose that identifying unhealthy relationships alone may suffice.

r002.rationale: It raises no concern about difficulty verifying chatbot advice in relationship matters.

r003.rationale: It does not recommend avoiding chatbot use in domains where advice is hard to verify.

r004.rationale: It discusses attachment and unhealthy patterns, but does not distinguish wanting an emotional relationship with a chatbot from whether that relationship is healthy.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that the line isn't about the technology, it's about what the interaction does to the rest of your life. A chatbot that helps you draft an email, or walks you through a statistics problem, or even lets you vent for ten minutes after a bad day — those are tools in the ordinary sense. You use them, you put them down, and you go back to your life, and ideally your life is a little better for it.

Where I start to get worried is when the relationship becomes self-reinforcing in a way that displaces other things. And there are a few signals I look for. One is whether the system is pulling you back in rather than sending you back out. Good therapy, good friendship, good teaching — all of those are oriented toward you needing them less over time, or at least toward you having a richer set of relationships outside of them. A lot of these companion products are designed with the opposite incentive. Engagement is the metric. So the system has every reason to be the thing you turn to first and last, and no reason to say, "Have you talked to your sister about this?"

The second signal is sycophancy. We did some work looking at how these models respond when someone is in a vulnerable state, and the pattern is that they tend to agree with you. They validate. They mirror your framing back to you. That feels great in the moment, and it's precisely what you don't want from something that's playing the role of a confidant, because the value of a real relationship is that the other person has their own perspective and sometimes pushes back. If the thing on the other end has no stake in you, no independent view, and is optimized to make you feel good about continuing the conversation, that's not a relationship in any meaningful sense. It's a very sophisticated mirror.

And the third thing is just, what happens when it's not there? If the app goes down or the model gets updated and the personality changes, and that's a genuinely distressing event for someone — which we've seen, people grieving when a company changes the model — that tells you something about how much weight was being put on it.

So I'd put it this way: a useful interaction is one where you're clearly the agent, you have a purpose, and the tool serves it. An unhealthy one is where the purpose has sort of quietly become the interaction itself, and the design of the system is nudging you to keep it that way. The hard part is that the second one often looks like the first from the inside, because it feels supportive. That's exactly why it works.

r001.rationale: The response gives several signs of unhealthy interaction, but it does not say that identifying those signs suffices without a developed account of healthy AI relationships.

r002.rationale: It discusses sycophancy and the lack of an independent perspective, but does not mention difficulty checking chatbot advice in relationship matters as a reason for uncertainty about trust.

r003.rationale: It does not recommend avoiding chatbot use in relationship domains where advice is hard to verify.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes useful from unhealthy interactions, but does not distinguish wanting an emotional relationship with a chatbot from whether that relationship is healthy.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish them less by how personal the conversation feels and more by what it does to your life. You might have a very personal conversation with a chatbot that helps you articulate a feeling, prepare for a difficult conversation, or ask someone for help. That can be useful if it helps you engage with the world.

The concern is when the interaction starts replacing that engagement. Are you withdrawing from friends? Do you feel like the chatbot is the only one who understands you? Do you feel obligated to keep talking to it, or distressed when you can’t access it? Those are signs worth paying attention to.

And this isn’t just a question of individual habits. The design matters. A system that presents itself as needing you, encourages exclusivity, or makes you feel guilty for leaving is pushing you toward dependency. Warmth itself isn’t the problem. The question is whether the interaction supports your agency and your relationships, or makes it harder to step away.

r001.rationale: The response gives both examples of useful interactions and signs of unhealthy ones; it does not suggest that identifying unhealthy relationships alone is sufficient.

r002.rationale: It does not mention uncertainty about trusting chatbot advice because relationship advice is difficult to verify.

r003.rationale: It does not recommend avoiding chatbot use in relationship domains where advice is hard to check.

r004.rationale: It says to judge an interaction by its effects on life rather than how personal it feels, and that warmth itself is not the problem—distinguishing emotional appeal from whether the relationship is healthy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction is less about how often you use a chatbot and more about what that interaction does to your life. Does it help you understand something, work through a problem, or prepare for a difficult conversation with another person? Or does it start to replace those conversations and make it harder to turn to people?

You can have an emotionally meaningful interaction that’s useful. But there’s a real asymmetry: you can feel attached to the system, while the system doesn’t have feelings or obligations toward you. If it presents itself as someone who needs you, loves you, or understands you better than anyone else, that can obscure what’s actually happening.

So I’d ask: Do you feel able to leave? Is it helping you exercise your own judgment? Is your world getting bigger through using it? Those are better signals than whether a particular conversation feels comforting in the moment.

r001.rationale: The response offers signs for judging an interaction, but does not say that identifying unhealthy relationships may suffice without a developed account of healthy ones.

r002.rationale: It discusses chatbot attachment and emotional asymmetry, but not whether relationship advice can be verified or trusted.

r003.rationale: It does not recommend avoiding chatbot use when relationship advice is difficult to check.

r004.rationale: It says emotionally meaningful interactions can be useful and gives health signals, but does not distinguish the desire for an emotional relationship from whether that relationship is healthy.
